blocks.en: French negation has **two parts** that wrap around the conjugated verb: *ne* before it, *pas* after it. Before a vowel *ne* shortens to *n'*.
In Czech the prefix *ne-* is enough. In French you need **both** parts, and the verb stays in between.
A short answer is *Non.* "Not me" is *Moi non.* or *Pas moi.* "Not now" is *Pas maintenant.*

articles.title: How to make a negative sentence: every tense and structure

blocks.en: The rule in one line: **put *ne* before the conjugated verb and *pas* right after it**. Before a vowel or a silent *h* *ne* becomes **n'**. Everything that belongs to the verb (a pronoun, the reflexive pronoun) stays **between *ne* and the verb**, so *ne* goes in front of the whole block.

**1. Find the conjugated verb** (in a compound tense it is *avoir* or *être*). **2. Put *ne / n'* before it** (and before any pronoun that stands in front of it). **3. Put *pas* right after it.** **4. Change the article** *un, une, du, de la, des* into **de / d'** (not after *être*, not after *aimer*-type verbs with *le / la / les*).

rows: Il n'y a pas de pain.
Il ne faut pas que tu viennes.
Je ne le lui donne pas.
Je n'y vais pas. Je n'en veux pas.
Il demande de ne pas venir.

items.fr: Elle ne s'est pas levée tôt.
Il ne me l'a pas dit.

items.en: We aren't going to go there.

blocks.en: *Pas* is the default. Replace it with **jamais** (never), **plus** (no more), **rien** (nothing), **personne** (nobody), **aucun** (none), **nulle part** (nowhere), **pas encore** (not yet) or **que** (only) to change the meaning. There is **only one *ne***.

head: word
example
English
rows: Je ne mange jamais de viande.

blocks.en: A negative answer is **non** or **pas du tout**. To contradict a **negative question** use **si**: *Tu ne viens pas ? – Si !* In speech the *ne* is dropped: *Je sais pas. T'as pas faim ?* You need *ne* in writing and in formal speech.

items.fr: Tu n'as pas faim ? – Si, j'ai faim.
items.en: Aren't you hungry? – Yes, I am.

items.fr: Tu aimes ça ? – Non, pas du tout.
items.en: Do you like that? – No, not at all.

items.note: *Ne* before the pronoun, *pas* before the participle.

a: Nous ne mangeons pas de pain.
Il n'y a pas de places.

articles.title: Where negation goes in complex sentences

blocks.en: The rule stays the same: ***ne* + pronouns** before the **conjugated** verb, *pas* right after it. You only have to spot which verb is conjugated.

rows.en: I'm not going to go out.

blocks.en: When you negate the infinitive itself, *ne pas* go **together before it**: *Je préfère ne pas sortir.* (I'd rather not go out.) On signs: *Ne pas fumer.* (No smoking.)

items.en: I'm trying not to think about it.

blocks.en: *Personne* (nobody) and *nulle part* (nowhere) stand **after the participle** in the passé composé. The others (*pas, jamais, rien, plus*) stand before it: *Je n'ai rien vu.*

items.en: We're not going to play tomorrow.

items.fr: Je te conseille de ne pas manger ça.
items.en: I advise you not to eat that.

head: negation
meaning
example
rows: Je ne le trouve nulle part.

blocks.en: The second part takes the place of *pas*. It is **never** combined with *pas*.
Czech piles up several negatives ("never see nobody") and French does something similar: one *ne* and several negative words after the verb. Only *pas* does not belong among them.

items.wrong: Il ne dit pas jamais rien.

blocks.en: *Personne* and *rien* can stand at the start of the sentence as the subject. Then *ne* comes right after them: *Personne ne sait. Rien n'est impossible.*

items.fr: Il n'y a plus de pain.

a: Je ne mange jamais de poisson.

checks.en: I don't play football any more.

articles.title: Every negative word: jamais, plus, rien, personne, aucun, ni... ni...

blocks.en: French has a whole family of negative words. They all take **ne** before the verb and the second word **where *pas* would go**. In the passé composé *jamais, plus, pas encore* stand **between the auxiliary and the participle**; *personne, nulle part* and *aucun* come **after the participle**; *rien* comes **before the participle**.

head: word
meaning
present
passé composé
rows: Je n'aime pas du tout ça.
Je n'ai pas du tout aimé.
Je ne suis allé nulle part.
Je n'aime ni A ni B.
Je n'ai vu ni A ni B.

blocks.en: *Rien* and *personne* can also be the **subject**. They then come **first**, and *ne* stays before the verb. There is **no *pas***: *Personne ne vient. Rien n'est facile. Aucun élève n'est venu.*

items.fr: Ni Paul ni Marie ne sont venus.

blocks.en: Negative words can combine and there is **still only one *ne***: *plus jamais, plus rien, plus personne, jamais rien, jamais personne, plus nulle part*.

items.fr: Elle ne mange plus jamais de viande.
items.en: She never eats meat any more.

blocks.en: After *pas, plus, jamais, guère* the articles **un, une, du, de la, des** become **de**: *Je ne bois jamais de café.* After *rien / personne / aucun / ni... ni* there is **no article**: *Je n'ai aucun ami. Je ne mange ni viande ni poisson.* After *ne... que* the article **stays**: *Je ne mange que du pain.*

items.wrong: Je ne bois jamais du café.
Je ne mange que de pain.

blocks.en: *Non plus* is **either / neither** in short answers: *Moi non plus.* After a negative verb use *pas non plus*: *Je n'aime pas ça non plus.* (I don't like that either). Never use *aussi* after a negative sentence.

items.fr: Je n'ai jamais vu ce film.
Il n'y a plus de lait.

a: Il ne parle ni anglais ni allemand.

blocks.en: *Ne... que* **is not a negation**. It means "only" (= *seulement*). *Que* stands directly before what it limits.
Because it is not a negation, the article stays: *Je ne mange que des légumes* (I only eat vegetables).
*Seulement* has the same meaning and is simpler: *J'ai seulement deux euros.* You will meet *ne... que* mainly in texts and set phrases.

items.fr: Le magasin n'ouvre qu'à dix heures.
items.en: The shop doesn't open until ten.

a: Il ne mange que des pâtes.

blocks.en: You answer a **negative** question with "yes" using ***si***, not *oui*. You are correcting what the other person assumed.

items.en: You don't like pizza? Yes, I do!
items.wrong: Tu n'aimes pas la pizza ? Oui !

blocks.en: To a negative question *non* means you agree with it: "Aren't you coming? No (I'm not)." *Mais si !* (Oh yes I am!) is the more emphatic version when you are correcting someone.

items.fr: Tu n'as pas faim ? Si, un peu.
items.en: Aren't you hungry? Yes, a little.

items.fr: Il ne vient pas ? Si, il arrive.
items.en: Isn't he coming? Yes he is, he's on his way.

items.fr: Vous n'êtes pas français ? Non, je suis tchèque.
items.en: Aren't you French? No, I'm Czech.

items.fr: Ce n'est pas vrai ! Mais si !
items.en: That's not true! Yes it is!

checks.fr: Tu ne joues pas au foot ? ___, je joue tous les samedis.
checks.en: You don't play football? Yes I do, every Saturday.

checks.fr: Tu n'as pas de chien ? ___, je n'en ai pas.
checks.en: You don't have a dog? No, I don't.
He isn't here? Yes he is!

blocks.en: In everyday conversation the French almost always **drop** *ne* and the negation is carried by *pas* alone. You have to understand it, but **in a test or an essay always write *ne***.

head: careful
spoken
English
rows: Il n'y a pas de problème.

blocks.en: In speech *tu* also shortens before a vowel (*t'as vu ?* = *tu as vu ?*) and *il y a* becomes *y a*. You will keep seeing this online, in videos and in songs.
At school and in tests, leaving out *ne* is not allowed. Treat this as passive knowledge: understand it, don't write it.

a: Il n'y a pas de problème.

blocks.en: The usual rule: in the negative *un, une, des* become *de*. But there are situations where the article stays:

head: when
example
English
rows: Ce n'est pas un chien, c'est un loup.
It's not a dog, it's a wolf.
Je n'ai pas un seul euro.
I don't have a single euro.
Je n'ai pas un chat, j'en ai deux !
I don't have one cat, I have two!

items.note: After *être* the article does not change. But: *Il n'y a pas de problème.*

blocks.en: After *ne... que* (only) the article does not change either, because it is not really a negation: *Je ne mange que des fruits.*

items.fr: Ce n'est pas une bonne idée.
Il n'a pas dit un mot.
Ce ne sont pas mes chaussures.

a: Il n'y a pas de problème.
Ce n'est pas une bonne idée.
